sections.topic: ERIK DEMAINE: All right, welcome back to 006 Data Structures. Today, we'
sections.emphasis: This lecture is one long build from motivation to a working in-place n log n sort, so keep the arc visible even though it's taught in one long stretch. Open with the interface: a priority queue is a subset of the set interface — insert an item with a key, and delete_max, remove and return the maximum-key item — motivated by routers prioritizing packets, schedulers picking the next process, or event simulation ordering by time. Note the audience already has a correct answer ready: a set AVL tree solves this in O(log n) per operation (O(n log n) to build, since build can't secretly use sorting), and augmenting it with a subtree-max property gets find_max down to constant time — 'so we're done, end of lecture,' Demaine says, and then explains why that's not actually the end: binary heaps get the same time bounds, build a log factor faster, and — the real payoff — are simple enough to give an in-place sorting algorithm, which AVL sort and merge sort cannot. Introduce priority-queue sort as the unifying frame before building the heap: insert every item, then repeatedly delete_max, then reverse — and plugging in different structures for the queue reproduces sorting algorithms already known: an unsorted array (insert is O(1), delete_max scans and swaps-with-last) reproduces selection sort; a sorted array (insert shifts into place, delete_max is O(1) at the end) reproduces insertion sort; set AVL reproduces AVL sort. Land why none of those are satisfying: the arrays are quadratic, and AVL sort, while O(n log n), is not in-place. State the goal precisely: an O(n log n), in-place sort, and say that's what a binary heap is built to deliver. Now build the structure itself. A complete binary tree fills every level except possibly the last completely, and left-justifies whatever nodes exist on that last level — and the key fact is that a complete binary tree of a given size n is unique, which is exactly what lets it be stored with no pointers at all, as a plain array in depth order (root, then its children, then their children, and so on — not the same order as an in-order traversal). Because the shape is fixed, the tree's structure is recoverable by arithmetic on array indices alone: for a node at index i, its children live at 2i+1 and 2i+2, and its parent lives at (i-1) div 2 — derive the 2i+1 rather than just asserting it, the way Demaine does from doubling the space at each depth and then correcting the off-by-one against the worked example. An index past the array's stored size simply means that child doesn't exist, which is only reliable because the tree is complete. Add the one remaining ingredient, the max-heap property: every node's key is greater than or equal to both its children's keys — a purely local constraint, unlike a binary search tree's global ordering, and prove the payoff explicit: by transitivity along any downward path, that local property forces every node to be greater than or equal to every node in its own subtree, so the maximum is always sitting at the root. Now the operations. Insert can only append at the array's end — the complete-tree analogue is the new last leaf on the last level — so after appending, run max_heapify_up: compare the new item with its parent, and if the child is bigger, swap them and recurse upward from the parent's old position; because only one item was ever out of place, each swap repairs exactly the one edge that could be wrong, and the process terminates in at most h swaps, so insert costs O(h) = O(log n). Delete_max is close to symmetric — Demaine even briefly says 'delete_min' out loud before catching himself and correcting to 'delete_max, thank you,' which is worth voicing as the live moment it is rather than smoothing over. The maximum is always at the root, and the only node an array can cheaply remove is the last one, so swap the root with the last leaf, then delete that last array slot — now the root holds whatever was at the last leaf, almost certainly too small — and run max_heapify_down: compare the out-of-place item with both its children, swap with whichever child is larger (swapping with the larger one, not the smaller, is what keeps both resulting edges satisfied), and recurse downward; this also costs O(h) = O(log n), amortized, since it rides on the array's amortized append/pop. Then make it in-place: rather than growing a fresh array, treat the input array A as fixed and let the heap Q be a growing-then-shrinking prefix of it — insert becomes just incrementing Q's size (the 'new' slot is already sitting there in A) plus a heapify-up, and delete_max becomes swap-to-the-front-of-the-remaining-prefix, decrement Q's size, plus a heapify-down; run every insert first and then every delete_max, and the items come out largest-first into the vacated suffix of the array, landing in increasing sorted order with no second array anywhere — this is heapsort. Close on the trick that makes build linear instead of O(n log n): rather than inserting items one at a time (which sums each node's depth, giving n log n, since depth grows with log n and most nodes are near the bottom), add all n items to the array at once with no heap property yet, then run heapify-down starting from the bottom of the tree and working up to the root. That sums each node's height instead of its depth — and since the vast majority of nodes are leaves with height 0, and only a few nodes near the root have height close to log n, that sum is linear rather than n log n. This is the piece that finally makes heapsort's O(n log n), in-place claim complete: linear build, logarithmic insert and delete_max, and the whole structure lives in one array.

quiz.question: Building a heap by inserting n items one at a time costs O(n log n), but building it by inserting all n items unheapified and then running heapify-down from the bottom up costs O(n). What is the key difference between the two that explains the gap?
options: One-at-a-time insertion sums each node's depth (bubbling up toward the root), while bottom-up heapify-down sums each node's height (bubbling down toward the leaves) — and since most nodes in a complete binary tree are leaves with height 0, that second sum is linear rather than n log n
The two approaches do the same total work; the bottom-up version is only faster because it skips the max-heap property check entirely
Bottom-up construction is faster because it only heapifies the bottom half of the array, leaving the top half unsorted until delete_max is called
quiz.explain: Inserting one at a time means every new item potentially bubbles all the way up to the root, and summing that over all n insertions is a sum of depths, which works out to n log n. Building bottom-up instead sums each node's height — how far it might have to sink — and because a complete binary tree has exponentially more nodes near the leaves than near the root, almost every node has small height: the sum of heights over the whole tree turns out to be linear in n, even though the sum of depths is not. Both approaches produce a fully correct heap; the asymmetry is purely about which quantity, depth or height, the total work ends up summing.

exercise.prompt: In the array-embedded heap, the node at index i has children at 2i+1 and 2i+2, and parent at (i-1) div 2. A node sits at array index 27. What index is its parent at?
exercise.explain: Parent(i) = (i - 1) div 2, using integer division. For i = 27: (27 - 1) div 2 = 26 div 2 = 13. You can check it the other direction too: index 13's children are at 2·13+1 = 27 and 2·13+2 = 28, so 27 is indeed one of index 13's children — consistent with the parent/child formulas being exact inverses of each other, the way Demaine derives them from the doubling-space argument and then the off-by-one correction against the worked example.
